layers.label: Galactic disk
layers.explanation: The thin, spinning plane of stars and gas — wider and smoother than the Milky Way's, with no central bar.

layers.label: Bright nucleus
layers.explanation: The dense center, glowing extra-bright and hosting a supermassive black hole of over 100 million solar masses.

hotspots.label: Central bulge
hotspots.description: The crowded, bright hub of Andromeda — brighter and rounder than our own galaxy's bulge.
hotspots.function: Shows where Andromeda's trillion stars crowd together.

hotspots.label: Smooth spiral arm
hotspots.description: A classic, smooth spiral arm — Andromeda is a textbook spiral with no central bar, unlike the Milky Way.
hotspots.function: Highlights what makes Andromeda a 'classic' spiral.

hotspots.label: Dust lanes
hotspots.description: Dark bands of dust and gas threading the arms — the raw material for new stars.
hotspots.function: Points out the dark dust that traces the arms.

hotspots.label: Satellite galaxies
hotspots.description: Two small companion galaxies, M32 and M110, that orbit Andromeda like moons orbit a planet.
hotspots.function: Shows that galaxies can have smaller galaxies circling them.

hotspots.label: Collision course
hotspots.description: The direction the Milky Way is falling toward Andromeda at about 110 kilometers per second — a merger in roughly four billion years.
hotspots.function: Marks the future merger path with our own galaxy.
